258.prule: Root-anchored, quantity-insensitive: primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the root (roots of 2+ syllables); stress does not shift with the addition or deletion of affixes, so prefix/suffix syllables are transparent and surface position varies with morphological composition; monosyllabic roots bear stress on the root syllable itself (o-'sa, mam-'sa); words with a root of 4+ syllables add secondary stress on the first syllable (word-initial in all cited examples; root-initial vs word-initial underdetermined since all examples are prefixless); small residue of unexplained/likely-borrowed exceptions with final or antepenult stress (8 items listed p.103). Not expressible as any single ^n pattern per word length.
258.srule: Roots of four or more syllables take a secondary stress on the first syllable in addition to the primary on the root penult (["kara'tupa], ["saka'hate-ne], ["kupa'naha-ne]); none described for shorter roots; root-initial vs word-initial not decidable (all examples prefixless).

259.dq: Stress is usually penultimate. Secondary stress occurs on the initial syllable and every other syllable thereafter. There are exceptions in which long vowels seem to attract stress. Phonetic cues for stress are intensity, pitch and duration. (Hore 1981)
259.dloc: the StressTyp2 entry (Hore 1981, no page given), StressTyp2 words wuˈrugu "billabong", ˌngalaaˈligi "turtle", ˌambalaˈlari "poor", ˈmuːn "foot"; exceptional maˈgaa, ˈd̯aalubu, waˌraarriˈwana
259.heavy: a long syllable (Hore's S:, i.e. a syllable with a long vowel ii/aa/uu): 'each S: forms a stress group of its own' and carries its stress; 'Word-final short syllables... are never stressed, while long syllables always are'; syllable closure and homorganic nasal-stop sequences (unit prenasalised stops) do not make a syllable heavy
259.dflt: penultimate primary stress with secondary stress on the first and alternate syllables, in words consisting of short syllables only
259.srule: Secondary stress on the first syllable and on the third, fifth etc.; in words with an odd number of short syllables the primary-stressed penult is preceded by two unstressed syllables; every long syllable forms its own stress group and is stressed (Hore 1981: 13-14). Word-initial 'SS: groups optionally front their stress (rule 14).
259.quote: The most obvious fact about stress on Nunggubuyu words is that for words with short syllables only, the normal situation is that the first and penultimate syllables are stressed as well as the third, fifth etc. syllables, depending on the length of the word. Where the number of syllables is odd, the penultimate syllable is preceded by two unstressed syllables. The penultimate syllable receives the primary stress. ... Long syllables can be accounted for quite easily. Basically, each S: forms a stress group of its own ... The S: usually retains the stress when this occurs. ... Word-final short …

259.sec_rule: In all-short-syllable words, secondary stress on the initial syllable and every second syllable thereafter (1, 3, 5...), counted from the left, never on the antepenult: 'lhala"wulbulg, 'burrumbu"rrunga, 'mara'garri"jinyung, 'rawu'rrumugu"rrumu; long-vowel syllables other than the primary carry secondary (dhu'maa.'mugu.'naa."murra); a polysyllabic suffix takes secondary on its first syllable ('ama.lha"gayag.'jinyung). Later reanalysis: Nyhuis 2023 (ch. 6) finds no alternating rhythm, only optional pitch accents at the left edges of morphological constituents plus a weight-sensitive AP-final accent.
259.sec_quote: for words with short syllables only, the normal situation is that the first and penultimate syllables are stressed as well as the third, fifth etc. syllables, depending on the length of the word. tn.quote: For this study, I conducted an analysis of intonational pitch accents and boundary tones in a corpus of three unscripted texts, following approaches in Autosegmental-Metrical Phonology (Ladd 2008) ... My analysis finds that pitch accents are most frequently anchored to the syllable aligned to the left edge of major morphological constituents, but appear to be in all cases optional, as reported for related languages of the area (Bishop & Fletcher 2005; Fletcher 2014). ... I suggest that these right-edge accents are associated with the penultimate mora of the Accentual Phrase

260.srule: None: "there is a maximum of one non-Low tone per noun in isolation" (p.48) and "there are no phonetic gradations of prominence in Kinyambo, as is found in many stress languages which have secondary (and sometimes tertiary) stress" (p.67). Bickmore's 'multiple stress levels' are four underlying strengths [0-3 stress] of the single root-initial stress (diagnosed by optional H, Phrase-final Destressing, Beat Deletion), not secondary stresses; two equal surface prominences occur only in inflected verbs and proper nouns (stressed prefix + stressed root, sec.3.4, 4.5.10) and phrase-medially by Beat Addition.

tn.quote: In Chapters Three and Four I will present evidence that while phonetically Kinyambo is a tone language (having a surface High/Low contrast), underlyingly it is a stress language best described in metrical terms. ... First, there is a maximum of one non-Low tone per noun in isolation. ... I will claim that prominence in Kinyambo is best represented as stress underlyingly. A late rule of Tone assignment will assign High and Low tone on the basis of the existing stresses. ... I propose that the domain of stress is the syllable, while the domain of tone is the mora.

261.dq: § 10. The rule for the accentuation of uncompounded words is the same in Old English as in the oldest period of the other Germanic languages, viz. the chief stress fell upon the stem-syllable and always remained there even when suffixes and inflexional endings followed it, as beran, to bear; dagas, days, greting, greeting; ...
261.dloc: Wright & Wright 1914:15-16 §10, Old English Grammar 2nd ed. — archive.org
261.srule: Secondary stress exists but Wright & Wright give no placement for simple words: 'The position of the secondary stress in trisyllabic and polysyllabic words fluctuated in OE.... it is impossible to formulate any hard and fast rules concerning it' (§10, p. 16); the secondary accent is as a rule separated from the primary by at least one syllable (§9, p. 13). In compound nouns the chief secondary stress falls on the syllable of the second element that would bear primary stress alone (brȳdguma, fēowergield), absent in obscured compounds (ēorod, hlāford) (§13, pp. 17-18). Later: Campbell 1959 §§87-92 (pp. 34-35) gives a weight-conditioned half-stress rule (heavy derivative suffixes and long final syllables made medial by inflexion are half-stressed only after a long syllable or its equivalent: æþelinges, singende, Hengestes vs cyninges, wesende).

morph.stmt: Old English inflection is entirely suffixal (case-number endings on nouns and adjectives, person-number, tense and mood endings on verbs, with root-internal ablaut/umlaut alternations as concurrent non-concatenative exponents), and derivation is mostly suffixal (-ung, -nes, -ere, -end, -ig, -ian...), but verbs and deverbal nouns also carry a closed set of unstressed 'inseparable particle' prefixes (ā-, be-, for-, ge-, of-, on-, oþ-, tō-; Wright §§645-656, Word-Formation) — in Wright's words, 'the chief stress fell upon the stem-syllable and always remained there even when suffixes and inflexional endings followed it' (§10) while 'the prefix ge- was already unaccented in the oldest period…

evidence_works.detail: A metrical-syntax study of Beowulf: it takes Old English word stress as primary on the first (root) syllable, with the trochaic Sx word as the norm and compounds carrying subordinate stress on the second element (Ss, Ssx, Sxs, Sxxs), and reports Kuhn's claim that Germanic word stress shifted to the first syllable in late Proto-Germanic. These stress facts are premises of the metrical argument, not findings; they agree with the catalog's fixed-initial entry for Old English (olde1238, Wright & Wright 1914, which the packet did not list) and add the compound secondary-stress patterns.

evidence_works.detail: A metrical essay with no measurements: it argues that Old English verse is a morphological, position-counting metre whose half-lines copy the leftmost-strong stress of native words, so the absence of promoted function words in OE verse is a metrical choice rather than evidence that OE lacked right-hand phrasal stress. It concludes that right-hand phrasal (Nuclear) stress and stress-timing features (vowel reduction, preference for monosyllabic dips) were most likely present in OE, which confirms the catalog's initial-stress entry and adds phrase-level detail.

evidence_works.detail: A foot-based Optimality Theory reanalysis of Old English word stress, taking its data from Campbell 1959 and Halle and Keyser 1971 (alliterative verse, loans, palatal diphthongization), with no measurements: primary stress is on the first syllable of a lexical word (prefixed verbs stress the root; ge- never stressed, for- and be- variable), the final syllable is never stressed, and secondary stress falls on a penultimate syllable preceded by one heavy or two light syllables, never after an initial light syllable. The proposed ranking is FT-FORM, NF, ALIGN HEAD >> ALIGN STEM, WSP >> PARSE-SYL

corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Oneida: primary stress on the penultimate syllable; no secondary stress". The source gives: Count back two vowels from the end of the (context-form) word, skipping final-syllable epenthetic -e- and stem-joiner -a-; accent that vowel (penult). If the penult vowel stands before a single non-h consonant (open penult), it is lengthened and the accent shifts to the following vowel (ultima). Before glottal stop or hR the laryngeal drops, the penult lengthens with falling tone and keeps the accent; before a cluster the penult keeps a short accented vowel. — StressTyp2 codes unconditional penult (STC P, rule 10 010 0010...).

263.heavy: Penult closed by a consonant cluster keeps the accent (short vowel); penult before glottal stop or h+resonant keeps the accent with laryngeal deletion and compensatory lengthening (falling tone); penult before a single non-h consonant (open penult) lengthens and the accent shifts to the following (final) vowel. Michelson (carried): 'The basic rule is to accent closed penults.' Heavy = closed syllable; Oneida has no underlying vowel-length contrast (length is derived by these rules).
263.dflt: final (accent shifts to the ultima whenever the penult is open, regardless of the ultima's shape; per Michelson only the penult lengthening depends on whether the ultima is closed)
263.prule: Count back two vowels from the end of the (context-form) word, skipping final-syllable epenthetic -e- and stem-joiner -a-; accent that vowel (penult). If the penult vowel stands before a single non-h consonant (open penult), it is lengthened and the accent shifts to the following vowel (ultima). Before glottal stop or hR the laryngeal drops, the penult lengthens with falling tone and keeps the accent; before a cluster the penult keeps a short accented vowel.
263.srule: None: 'Every word has an accent mark... No word has more than one accent mark' (Abbott 2006, Part I p. 12; the lengthened 'dragged' syllable before the accent is vowel length, not a second stress). StressTyp2 likewise codes secondary stress Absent ('There is no secondary stress').

263.exq_: Because these rules have few exceptions ... they are not foolproof. Some exceptions can be explained as part of historical processes ... [p. 40] -kó ... It is always accented. This is an exception to the regular accent rules ... [-kʌ́] This suffix is always accented
263.tone: Abbott describes no lexical tone; pitch is a correlate of the single word accent ('straight accent': louder and slightly higher pitch). An accented vowel lengthened by loss of a following glottal stop or of h before l/y/w/n is 'given a falling tone' (accent mark plus raised dot); a 'dragged' (pre-accentual lengthened) syllable has 'an even tone'. For tone the entry now rests on Julian 2010, quoted in the tone block.

264.srule: Secondary stress on alternating syllables after the initial primary: on the 3rd syllable in 3- and 4-syllable words; in words of 5 or more syllables on the 3rd or the 5th syllable or both (the six-syllable examples á.ri.mà.ge.à.ke, mét.o.kàn.i.kè.te carry both); disyllables carry primary stress only.
264.quote: Primary stress occurs regularly on the first syllable of stress group while secondary stress falls on subsequent alternating syllables. Juncture (indicated by space) is the boundary of the stress group. ... Stress is predictable. ... Three and four syllable words carry primary stress on the initial syllable and secondary stress on the third syllable.

morph.rootq: Phinnemore 1985 Sec.1 p.174: 'Primary stress occurs regularly on the first syllable of stress group while secondary stress falls on subsequent alternating syllables. Juncture (indicated by space) is the boundary of the stress group.' The domain is the word/stress group, not the root; the illustrating words are inflected verbs and possessed nouns (a.ri.le 'I went', me.si.ke.ne 'you will sit', o.kan.mai.le 'I am doing it', a.ri.ma.ge.a.ke 'he always goes', de.ne 'my eye'), all root-initial because the language has no prefixes, so root-initial and word-initial coincide.
morph.elicq: Phinnemore 1985 p.174: 'Stress is predictable. The following examples were observed in words up to five syllables in length.' (method not stated; data 'gathered during periodic field trips between 1972 and 1980', p.173). The only contextual remark is phrase-level: 'Monosyllabic words occuring at the beginning of a noun phrase carry stress but stress on the word following will be lenis ... In the sequence ŋei, ŋerep men, women, with an intervening pause, both carry stress but in the same sequence without the pause, ŋei ŋerep people, only the first syllable takes the stress.'
morph.stmt: Ono is described as exclusively suffixing/encliticising: verbs are 'Stem - I (aspect -mage-, -okan-) - II (tense -mai-, -i-, -ko-, -ike-) - III (person-number)' with 'the suffixes... ranked according to the distance from the stem' (Phinnemore 1985 App. E p.204-205), object markers and medial switch-reference/person suffixes likewise follow the stem ('The order of suffixes is the same as on final verbs', Phinnemore 1988 p.105); on nominals 'There are relatively few suffixes added to non-verbs. These suffixes are possession, number, a diminuative, and a locative. Case and emphatic markers are attached to free pronouns' (1985 p.196), with possessive, locative, comitative and ergative marked…

265.dq: Main stress is normally penultimate, but can be final or antepenultimate under special circumstances. It can be analyzed with a syllabic trochee, with stressed suffixes and extrametrical suffixes.
265.dloc: Hayes 1995, Metrical Stress Theory, p. 266, sect. 6.3.11 (c) Onondaga (the page the StressTyp2 entry pins); Abrams 2006, p. 12 fn. 7 and sect. 1.5, pp. 19-20.
265.srule: Even-numbered syllables counted from the beginning of the word up to the main stress are metrically strong (left-to-right 'even iambs'); the pretonic span is 'the domain of the secondary stress rule'. Stated by Hayes as a metrical analysis of pretonic vowel lengthening in even-numbered syllables (Chafe 1977; Michelson 1988 sect. 3.4.2), not as transcribed audible secondary stresses.

tn.quote: 3.4.1. Separation of Pitch and Stress The most intriguing accentual development unique to Onondaga is that the highest pitch of a word can occur on a different syllable from the strongest stress; that is, whereas stress and pitch are both realized on the same syllable in all the other LI languages, pitch and stress have separated in Onondaga. This was first noted by Woodbury (cited in Chafe, 1977a, pp. 173-75). Interestingly, the position of high pitch versus strong stress is not dependent on any of the other accent-related developments of Onondaga ...

qtr.text: § 4. Word stress is musical-dynamic [pitch plus force], falling, as a rule, on the final syllable of the word. In individual speech one meets unstressed pronunciation of the suffixal particles that close the word, and sometimes of case suffixes as well. In these cases the stress turns out to be on the second or third syllable from the end.

266.dq: § 4. Словесное ударение — музыкально-силовое, падающее, как правило, на конечный слог слова. В индивидуальной речи встречается безударное произношение замыкающих слово суффиксальных частиц, а иногда и падежных суффиксов. В этих случаях ударение оказывается на втором или третьем от конца слоге.

267.srule: Simple words: a secondary stress tends to fall on the third syllable (not easily heard unless that syllable contains a stop or /a/). Reduplicated and compound words: secondary stress on the first syllable of the second root. (Larsen & Larsen 1977:12 sec. 5.1; restated Larsen & Larsen 1982:77 sec. 1.3 'the second greatest emphasis is on the third syllable in words longer than two syllables'. The record's primary source, Healey et al. 1969:34, does not mention secondary stress.)
267.quote: The first syllable of each Orokaiva word is stressed. When h occurs between unstressed vowels it is very light, and sometimes seems to be quite silent. Its phonemic status in these positions needs investigating in each main dialect.

morph.rootq: "The first syllable of each Orokaiva word is stressed. When h occurs between unstressed vowels it is very light, and sometimes seems to be quite silent." (§1 Phonology, p.34). The domain named is the word, not the root/stem; note also p.34: "The apparent exceptions (ra indicative, re interrogative, rate 'but' and rami 'kind of') are probably enclitics and pronounced as part of the preceding word."
morph.elicq: No statement of how stress was determined. The only methodological remarks are: "In June 1967 the authors spent two weeks investigating Orokaiva verbs and preparing some preliminary language lessons for use of missionaries in the Orokaiva area." (p.33) and "The Orokaiva examples are provided with normal English capitalization and punctuation, since intonation has not been analyzed." (p.34).
morph.stmt: Almost exclusively suffixing: "Verbs consist of a stem... followed by up to four suffixes to indicate tense, subject person-and-number, and mood" (p.35); the only prefix described is a partial-reduplicative plural-stem prefix ("by the use of a reduplicative prefix or a suffix or both", p.35; also on a few nouns/adjectives p.46), while "Most nouns are uninflectable" (p.46) and grammatical relations are carried by postpositions that follow the noun phrase (p.48).

sources.text: "In both Orokolo and Toaripi, with words of two or three syllables, the stress is normally on the penultimate syllable. There are some exceptions, the most notable being with the nominative form of the personal pronouns: ara /ará/ I, are /aré/ 'he', 'she', 'it'; ere /eré/ 'they'. ... With words of four or more syllables, the syllable two removed from the main penultimate stress has a minor stress, e.g. karikara /kàrikàra/ 'village'. The stress of the stem is repeated in reduplicated words, e.g. hirihiri /hírihíri/ 'dirty', hohorohohoro /hohórohohóro/ 'radiance'." (Brown 1986:xiv)

268.srule: Words of four or more syllables carry one minor (secondary) stress on the syllable two before the main penultimate stress, e.g. karikara 'village' (kà.ri.ká.ra; Brown 1986 prints /kàrikàra/, Brown 1973: 307 /karikára/ under the same rule). Reduplicated words repeat the stem's stress (hírihíri, hohórohohóro = 010010). Iteration of the minor stress in longer non-reduplicated words is not stated.

270.cfw: Gerdel's first-hand descriptions (1973, 1985, 1990, and her pronunciation notes in Slocum 1986) consistently call Páez stress contrastive and anchored to the root (wála 'big' vs wakú 'tick', trisyllabic roots stressed medially, some verb suffixes attracting the stress), and the only dissent is Gordon's 2002 survey listing of penultimate stress and Mondelli's 2014 one-speaker amplitude measurements suggesting weak initial stress in disyllabic nouns, both far weaker than the primary description.

excx.exc_elsewhere_quote: the word stress in Pagu can be said not always to occur in the penultimate but also in the final position. This determined by four factors: (i) the speed of the speech (normal/rapid vs slow) (ii) the two types of the adjacent vowels (identical vs different vowels) and (iii) the position of the vowels in the words (final or prefinal), and (iv) the heaviness of the syllable. Langdon 1977:239 (carried, not re-read): "the great number of derivational prefixes and the very small number of derivational suffixes".

273.cfw: Ferrell 1982, Chang 2006, Chen 2009, Yeh 2017 and Shih 2018 all give penultimate stress as the general Paiwan rule, and the only departures they report are monosyllables, hiatus-derived heavy final syllables, and the shift off a penultimate schwa onto the final syllable in the central villages (Piuma and its neighbours), which are exceptions inside the last two syllables rather than a different system.

evidence_works.detail: For the Piuma dialect the article reports (after Shih 2019b) that penultimate stress shifts to the final syllable whenever the penult holds a schwa, and relays Shih's acoustic finding that this penultimate schwa is much shorter and more variable than other vowels. The catalog's fixed-penultimate Paiwan entry (Ferrell 1982) has no such exception, so this is a dialect-level refinement, though the measurements are Shih's, not this article's.

274.srule: Only in compounds/derived words and at sentence level: in verb compounds and zero-derived (verbalized) words the rightmost member's final syllable carries primary stress and the final syllables of the preceding member words carry secondary stress ('secondary stress, if there is any, precedes' the word-final primary); in the sentence the verb's final syllable is primary and the final syllables of other lexical words secondary, clitics tertiary. No secondary stress is described inside a simple word.

275.dq: Every alternate mora is stressed. The first gets main stress in words without long vowels (diphthongs count as one mora). If the second vowel is long and the first is short, primary stress falls on the second syllable. If the final vowel should get a secondary stress according to the alternate count, it optionally receives that stress, if it does not the vowel is devoiced. (Dayley 1989:435)

275.heavy: a long vowel in the second syllable when the first vowel is short (long vowels and two-vowel clusters count as two morae; diphthongs ai/oi count as one mora); separately, a geminate stop or s after the first root vowel also permits (variably) second-mora primary stress
275.prule: Primary stress on the first mora of the word; 'usually' on the second mora instead when the second syllable has a long vowel and the first a short vowel, but in that case placement 'often varies' between first and second; second mora also 'frequently' primary when the first vowel is a prefix vowel, and 'may be' primary after a root-initial CV followed by a geminate stop or s (variable).
275.srule: Secondary stress on every other mora after the primary-stressed mora, 'only slightly less' than primary (long vowels = two morae, ai/oi = one); a secondary due on the second half of a long vowel is realised on the beginning of that vowel and the following vowel is then stressed; a word-final secondary is optional in phrase-final position (if absent the final vowel is devoiced); in most compounds the count begins anew on the second stem, whose first stressed mora is only secondary.

corr.head: StressTyp2's coding matches the source only in part
corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Paraujano: In words of all sizes, primary stress falls on the peninitial syllable." The source gives: If the first syllable of the word is light, the second syllable is tonic; if the first syllable is heavy (long vowel, diphthong, or closed), the first syllable itself is tonic. — StressTyp2 (entry, via Gordon 2002 < Patte 1989) codes quantity-insensitive peninitial stress in toto; the source's rule gives peninitial only when sigma-1 is light and initial when sigma-1 is heavy, so StressTyp2 captures one branch and misses the weight condition.

morph.rootq: Álvarez 2009 §2 p.133: 'Es posible determinar automáticamente la sílaba tónica de una palabra: (1) Si la primera sílaba es liviana, la segunda sílaba es la tónica: a.tü.kü.raa ‘despertarse’, pa.ya.wi ‘contento’, a.wee.ta ‘nacer’; y (2) Si la primera sílaba es pesada (esto es, tiene una vocal larga, un diptongo, o es trabada), ella misma es la tónica: jaa.pü.chi.kai ‘el niño’, tou.ya.pei ’lo pido’, wat.taa ‘mañana’. Patte (1989) registra algunos pocos casos en los que estas reglas no parecen funcionar: jü.rü.kó ‘todo’, taü.rí ‘fuera de mí’, kee.tí.chi ‘aunque’, etc.' — the rule is stated over the word from its left edge; the illustrative forms include prefixed words…
morph.elicq: Álvarez 2009 p.131: 'Este artículo en particular se fundamenta en el procesamiento de dichas fuentes escritas con el objeto de presentar, de modo panorámico, generalizaciones fonológicas, morfológicas y sintácticas acerca de la lengua a partir de los datos mejor documentados. Sobresalen así los ejemplos tomados directamente de Patte (1989)...' and p.133 'Patte (1989) registra algunos pocos casos en los que estas reglas no parecen funcionar'. The stress rule is a secondary restatement of Patte's 1973-1981 fieldwork description (Patte 1978 Amerindia 3; Patte 1989 EDLA); neither Álvarez 2009 nor Álvarez & Bravo 2008 says whether it rests on isolated words, frames, texts or measurements.
morph.stmt: Añú has a single prefix position — the seven personal prefixes ta-/pü-/nü-/jü-/wa-/ja-/na- (or indefinite a-, or derivational ka- 'tener') marking possessor on nouns, subject on active verbs and the term of prepositions ('los verbos activos son obligatoriamente prefijables y los estativos son obligatoriamente imprefijables', Álvarez 2009 p.137) — while everything else is suffixal: possessed-state -e on alienable nouns, article/definiteness and number -ka-i/-ka-rü/-ka-nü, tense-aspect and gender-number agreement (-ee, -iya, -atü + -i/-ü/-in, -chi/-rü/-nü), desiderative -ee, negation -pe, conditional -ye/-ri, subordinator -i, causative -ira, passive -üwa, reflexive -awa, augmentative -raa…

277.sec_quote: Es posible determinar automáticamente la sílaba tónica de una palabra [...] — the whole §2 Fonología (pp. 132–133: phoneme inventory, vowel length, syllable weight, the tonic-syllable rule, vowel harmony) was read; it speaks only of 'la sílaba tónica' (one tonic syllable per word) and contains no mention of secondary, rhythmic or alternating stress; a full-text search of the article for secundari/acento/ritm finds only 'predicción del acento' in the abstract and conclusion.

ev.cite: Pease & Betts 1971 Parintintin phonology, Tupi Studies I p.10 §5.1 (archive.org sil-tupi-studies "presented as a tentative analysis"); StressTyp2 entry boilerplate only
ev.text: 5.1. Phonological Phrase. A phonological phrase is postulated to account for certain features of stress, pitch, and length which are commonly associated with groups of syllables. The phonological phrase is composed of one or more syllables, generally more than one. In a series of syllables comprising a phonological phrase one syllable occurs with higher pitch and with more stress than the others. This is termed 'phrase stress'. Stress. Phrase stress generally occurs on the first syllable of the phrase except in initial phrases in a sentence, in which case one or two unstressed syllables may precede the stressed syllable

278.srule: Not mentioned in Pease & Betts 1971 (sections 1-5, pp. 1-12; the only second stress described is a sentence-level one, p. 11), Betts 1981 (Chave de Pronuncia, p. 8), Betts 2012 or dos Santos 2024 (section 3.2.1). Marcoli 2018 p. 123 records a secondary stress only in some compounds/derivations whose suffix or second member has its own tonic syllable: the root keeps its stress as secondary ([ika'tu] + [e'te] -> [ika,tue'te] 'muito bom', [pa,kou'hu] 'banana nanica'); no rhythmic secondary stress in simple words is described.

278.sec_quote: In some sentences heavy stress occurs at two points. The second of these is always on the last or next to last syllable of the sentence and does not necessarily coincide with phrase stress. In such cases, the second stress appears to mark the addition of a construction to a sentence which would be grammatically complete without it.

279.quote: The accentation of words is subject to nearly the same rules as in the English language; dissyllables have the accent on penultima, in words of three or more syllables, it rests on antipenultima; as: kátta, club, márniti, good, wayándata. The latter of these rules however is not observed in the conjugation of verbs which are apt to retain the accent on the first or second syllable of the root, even when followed by more than two syllables; as ngúkaintyanna, ngukáintyaranna.

Adelaide: University of Adelaide Press. DOI 10.20851/barngarla. morph.rootq: Clendon 2015 contains no statement about word stress or accent (adjudicator grep of the full text for stress|accent|prosod returns nothing; 'syllable' occurs only in phonotactic/verb-root-shape remarks, e.g. p.? 'Barngarla verb roots may (usually at least) contain only two syllables'; Ch.2 'Writing Barngarla sounds' covers consonants, rhotics, vowels and sandhi only). Schürmann's 1844 spellings occasionally carry accent marks that Clendon reproduces without comment (e.g. 'ngammiá' in (4.2), 'Marrályinga ... píttanarrù kányanga' in (7.3)). The catalog's stress coding for this language rests on Hayes 1995:205 / Gordon 2002, not on this grammar.
morph.elicq: No stress description in the source. For context on the evidential base of the whole grammar: 'This commentary will seek to recast the first twenty-two pages of Clamor Schürmann's 1844 Vocabulary of the Parnkalla language in the light of contemporary understandings about other Thura-Yura languages' (p.1) — all data are philological reinterpretation of a written 1844 missionary source; no speakers were recorded for this work.
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing: 'Barngarla verbs are composed of a base or ROOT, to which are added various endings or suffixes that show when and sometimes how the event or act portrayed by the verb is being performed' (§4.1 p.37); 'For lots of the meanings that English conveys by way of prepositions... Barngarla uses suffixes' (Ch.7 p.71); 'Suffixes are used in Barngarla for many purposes' (Ch.8 p.95) — the only 'prefixes' mentioned are frozen demonstrative/interrogative formatives i-/ngu-/nga-/wa- on the base -nha (Ch.9 p.111), and negation is a free preverbal particle guda.

281.prule: Primary stress on the antepenultimate syllable in words of three or more syllables (quantity-insensitive: CVV syllables count like CV); Everett places it on the final syllable in disyllables (oní, pahá), where the record's other source (Chapman & Derbyshire 1991:348 via StressTyp2) conflicts.
281.srule: Secondary stress falls on every odd-numbered syllable counted from the right edge of the word (the final syllable and alternate syllables leftward; iambic feet built right-to-left, a word-initial leftover syllable also stressed), e.g. bóvirì, kajóvirì, ìtarápahà, katàrarárakì. In reduplicated forms the reduplicant's secondary stress may fall on either of its two syllables.
281.quote: For the moment, let us assume that Paumari syllables are always of the shape CV or CVV and that they are always monomoraic. This enables us to state the preliminary generalizations about Paumari stress placement in (1) and (2): (1) Secondary stress is placed on every odd-numbered mora from right-to-left. 281.sec_rule: Secondary stress on every odd-numbered syllable counted from the right word edge (right-to-left quantity-insensitive iambs, degenerate foot allowed word-initially): the final syllable and every second syllable to the left of the antepenultimate primary, e.g. bóvirì, kajóvirì, ìtarápahà, katàrarárakì; bimoraic words carry one stress only.
281.sec_quote: (1) Secondary stress is placed on every odd-numbered mora from right-to-left. [...] 3.4. Foot structure and secondary stress ... All feet on the lowest layer (secondary stress) are iambic – right-headed, binary groups of syllables ... Moreover, all feet are oriented towards the right edge of the word. To use a process metaphor, they are built from right to left. [...] (31) (kajó)(virì) 'island' (32) (à)(haká)(barà) 'dew'

sources.text: "1.2.6. Accent. One additional feature of Pawnee speech is that of accent or stress. This feature does not seem to be phonemic, since there are no examples of it establishing morphemic contrasts. With polysyllabic nouns and particles, stress generally, though not always, falls on the first syllable. With verb forms, however, the placement of stress is more variable. What the conditioning factors for its placement are is not known at this time, and for this reason there will be no attempt at accounting for it." (Parks 1976:17)

morph.stmt: Parks & Pratt 2008:29 fn.8: 'As well as being numerous, the grammatical categories of the verb are largely marked by prefixes'; p.44: 'Only two categories are marked by suffixes: aspect and subordination'; nouns, by contrast, take only suffixes for case, (body-part) plural and derivation (-uʔ, -kis, -kusuʔ; pp.30-31) — i.e. a heavily prefixing polysynthetic verb (26-slot prefix/proclitic template before the stem, 3 suffix slots after) with a lightly suffixing noun.

283.sec_rule: Rhythmic secondary prominence on the heads of iambic feet built from left to right: in words of open (light) syllables the 2nd, 4th, 6th... syllables from the beginning of the word, realised as iambic vowel lengthening (Taurepang: also high pitch); closed CVC (and long-vowel) syllables are heavy and always foot heads, the count restarting after them; the final syllable carries the main stress. (Alvarez 1997 states this as foot construction and duration, without the term 'acento secundario'; Pessoa 2006 calls the 2nd/4th syllables 'acentuadas'.) Not mentioned in Armellada & Olza 1999, 'Observaciones' (front matter, the page read).

284.srule: Amini 1997: besides the main (final) stress, multi-syllabic words and compounds carry lesser secondary and tertiary stresses 'which can be counted from the direction of stress'; her metrical analysis parses syllabic iambs right-to-left (e.g. hà.fe.zé), i.e. on alternate syllables leftward from the final. No data with marked secondaries are given, so the rule string marks the primary only.

284.sec_rule: None at word level per the latest dedicated study: 'no secondary stresses at word level' (Hosseini 2014). The primary source Amini 1997 had posited secondary stress on every second syllable counted leftward from the final main stress (right-to-left syllabic iambs with degenerate feet: qà.lam.hấ 'pens', ge.ràn.ta.rín 'most expensive'), an analysis Hosseini 2014 names and rejects; Kahnemuyipour 2000 fn. 6 calls the status of Persian secondary stress 'quite unclear'.
284.sec_quote: p. 3 fn. 7: "It should be mentioned that multi-syllabic words as well as compounds have also secondary stress which can be counted from the direction of stress." p. 7 (18a): "Foot Construction ... Parse words into Syllabic Iambs going from right to left"; p. 15: "ranking of Parse-Syll over Ft-Bin results in the selection of the grammatical candidate, i.e., [(qà)(lam.hấ)]"
284.sec_loc: Hosseini section 3.2 p. 26 and Table 2 row i p. 12; Amini fn. 7 p. 3, (18)-(19) p. 7, Tableaux 3-4 pp. 15-16; Kahnemuyipour fn. 6 pp. 124-125

tn.quote: Phonologically, the Persian syllabic prominence consists of a H tone, and from a distributional perspective it is an accent [3][4]. … Note that in Persian all accents at the phrase or clause level are phonologically equal [4]. In addition to the syntactically driven accent H, there are two boundary tones in the language: L% for declaratives and Wh-questions, and H% for yes/no questions. … This paper has argued that prominence in Persian words, generally described as ‘word stress’, is manifested by a tone whose position is governed by the syntax.
tn.cite: Rahmani, Hamed. 2018. Persian 'word stress' is a syntax-driven tone. Proceedings of the 6th International Symposium on Tonal Aspects of Languages (TAL 2018), 18-20 June 2018, Berlin, pp. 155-158. ISCA. doi:10.21437/TAL.2018-31
tn.locator: p. 155 (sec. 1 'Word prominence in Persian'), p. 157 (end of sec. 2.3) and p. 158 (sec. 3 'Conclusions')
tn.note: One accent per word, realised as an H tone on a syllable fixed by morphosyntax (final in nouns) and cued by f0 alone; not stored in the lexicon; no separate stress; boundary tones L% and H%.

evidence_works.work: Sadat-Tehrani 2008, The intonational grammar of Persian (PhD thesis, University of Manitoba: xvii+298 pp.; §1.3 pp. 22-25, §7.1 pp. 162-163)
evidence_works.detail: Same placement as the catalog rule: 'For nouns, adjectives, and most adverbs, the stress is word-final' (p. 22); polymorphemic words 'have final stress' (p. 22); verbs 'have their stress on the final syllable of the main constituent, i.e., the present stem, the past stem, or the participle' (p. 23). Adds detail to the record's verb-prefix exception: 'the negative marker ne-/næ-, the durative prefix mi-, and the subjunctive/imperative prefix be- attract the stress... ne-/næ- takes precedence over mi-' (p. 24, ex. (21) né-mi-xær-id-æm); 'The future tense, exceptionally, has the stress on the final syllable of the auxiliary' (p. 24, xah-ǽm-ræft); compound verbs 'are stressed on the non-verbal element' (p. 24; ex. (23) geryé+kærd on p. 25). Clitics outside the domain: 'Enclitics and certain suffixes such as the indefinite marker -i (as in ketáb-i "a book") do not affect stress' (p. 25). Lexical exceptions as in the record's exc_quote: 'There are a few morphologically simple words, mostly of Arabic origin, which are stressed word-initially. Examples include ǽmma "but", and bǽle "yes"' (p. 25). Vocatives: 'the consultants unanimously judged the stress for citation forms on the ultimate syllable and for vocatives on the initial syllable' (p. 163; the test is described on p. 162). No statement on secondary stress.

evidence_works.work: Mumm 2007, Strukturkurs Neupersisch: SoSe 2007 (LMU München course script: 70 pp.; copy read is the revised 'Stand: Januar 2009' version, 71 pp., §2.3 pp. 35-36)
evidence_works.detail: Same final-syllable rule as the record: '2.3.1. Regel: Alle Wörter des Np. sind auf der letzten Silbe betont (oxyton); Suffixsilben gehören dazu genauso wie Stammsilben: pedár "Vater" - pedarā́n "Väter" - pedarāné "väterlich"' (p. 35). Adds the suffix-vs-enclitic diagnostic: 'Enklitika werden im Unterschied zu Suffixen nicht betont: xāné-rā "das Haus (Obj.)", xāné-ī "ein Haus"... Enklitika nehmen an dieser Regel nicht teil und ziehen den Ton nicht auf sich' (p. 35); verbal exceptions: 'Nicht betont sind die Personalendungen des Präteritums, dominant betont sind die Präfixe mī- und na- und alle Präverbien' (p. 35); initially stressed items: 'Ausnahmen: erstsilbenbetont (baryton) sind: einzelne arab. LW: ámmā "aber", válī... yáʿnī "das heißt", bále "ja" u.a.; einige persische Konjunktionen bzw. Partikeln...: mágar..., hár čand (ke)..., mábādā..., ágarče' (p. 36); diachronic origin in a penult law of late Old / early Middle Persian (§2.3.2, p. 36). No statement on secondary stress.

evidence_works.work: Ghomeshi 1997, Projection and inflection: a study of Persian phrase structure (PhD thesis, University of Toronto: ix+301 pp.; copy read dated 1996; §1.3.1 pp. 17-18)
evidence_works.detail: 'In Persian stress generally occurs on the final syllable of a word' (p. 17); 'Stress falls on the final syllable of the stem. Affixes that affect stress placement are the plural suffix on nouns, the comparative and superlative suffixes on adjectives, and the suffixes of nominal derivation. In each case stress appears on the final syllable of the suffix' (p. 18, ex. (11)-(12) ketâb-hâ, ketâb-che-hâ, kuchek-tarin). On compounds: 'In compound nouns the main stress falls on the final syllable of the second element with the final syllable of the first element carrying a secondary stress. In very common compounds the secondary stress disappears' (p. 18, ex. (13) fârsi zabân, tâze vâred). This compound-internal secondary stress is Lazard's statement reported secondhand; it concerns the first member of a compound, not the word-level iterative secondary stress that Amini 1997 posited and Hosseini 2014 rejected, and Amini fn. 7 already records that 'compounds have also secondary stress'.

evidence_works.work: Rahmani, Rietveld & Gussenhoven 2016, Persian word accent is deletable (Proc. Speech Prosody 2016, Boston: 440-444, doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2016-90)
evidence_works.detail: Placement statement, p. 440: 'Accentual minimal pairs of phonological words are highly frequent, mainly due to a rule which assigns an accent to the final syllable of morphological words, skipping right-edge clitics [2]. An example is /vɒnet/ [vɒ.nét] "pickup" vs. /vɒn-et/ [vɒ.net] "your bathtub".' Measured: time-normalized F0 (Praat, 12 points per syllable) on the minimal pair [tɒ.béʃ] 'proper name' vs [tɒ.beʃ] 'his swing' with copular clitic -e in two carrier frames ([un tɒbeʃ-e], [midunam tɒbeʃ-e]), read by 8 university-educated native speakers (4 m, 4 f, aged 27-37; 80 sentences) under neutral, contrastive-focal, post-focal, asserted and presupposed conditions elicited by mini-dialogues; plus an identification experiment with 22 listeners scored by d-prime against a JND baseline. Findings: 'Accented syllables are substantially higher than their unaccented counterparts in neutral and focal pronunciations of Focus A and in asserted pronunciation of Focus B' (p. 441); 'The results of two experiments confirmed that accents are deleted. A production experiment showed low F0 plateaus on the post-focal and presupposed words, while perception experiment showed that deaccented members of minimal pairs are not recognized above the just-noticeable-difference (JND) baseline' (p. 443); 'Persian, having no phonetic stress [1], represents a clear case of a language that neutralizes the accent contrast' (p. 443). Supports the record's tone_cls 'pitch-accent'; no statement on secondary stress.

evidence_works.work: Abolhasanizadeh 2012, F0 as the dominant cue to accent location in Persian (Proc. Speech Prosody 2012, Shanghai: 551-554, doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2012-139)
evidence_works.detail: Placement, §2 p. 551: 'Stress assignment is straightforward. Final syllables of nouns, adjectives, most adverbs and unprefixed verbs have the stress [8, 10]. Prefixed verbs take stress on the prefix.' Clitic exclusion: 'Persian presents minimal stress pairs because clitics are not included in the domain for stress assignment, which attracts a stress on the last syllable' (p. 551); 'the assignment of a pitch accent to final syllables of phonological words skips right-edge clitics, but not suffixes' (p. 552, citing Lazard 1957: 48 and Shaqaqi 1993: 46). Material and method: source utterances un tɒˈbeʃ-e 'that is light' (word) and un ˈtɒb-eʃ-e 'that is his swing' (word + clitic) recorded from two educated male speakers of standard Persian in Tehran; Praat resynthesis of nine F0 steps on the second syllable [beʃ] (20 Hz steps 60-220 Hz in Exp. I; 10 Hz steps 160-70 Hz in Exp. II); identification and discrimination tests with 51 listeners (30 f, 21 m, aged 23-38) in Exp. I and 30 listeners (18 f, 12 m, aged 19-35) in Exp. II. Result: 'The results showed a complete perception shift from one condition to the next, with responses of 100% and 0% for at least one stimulus on each side of the switch point' (p. 552 for Exp. I, repeated for Exp. II on p. 553; switch points 130 Hz and 125 Hz by logistic regression). Conclusion, p. 554: 'This strongly suggests that Persian has a pitch accent and that it has no stress in the sense of either a segmentally privileged position, as in English, or a syllable with phonetically enhanced segmental, as in Spanish.... In the case of Persian, that syllable is structurally defined as the last syllable of the non-cliticized word.' Supports the record's tone_cls 'pitch-accent'; no statement on secondary stress.

evidence_works.work: Sadeghi 2017, The timing of pre-nuclear pitch accents in Persian (Journal of the International Phonetic Association 49(3): 305-329 (print volume dated 2019; first pub)
evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: An instrumental intonation study finding that the rising pitch accent on a Persian stressed syllable starts its L at the onset of the stressed syllable and reaches its H about 10 ms into the first post-accentual vowel regardless of syllable structure or vowel length, with the H pulled earlier in penult- and final-stressed words but not by a following accent. It restates the final-stress rule and its prefix and enclitic exceptions from Ferguson 1957 and Kahnemuyipour 2003 rather than testing stress placement, so it adds the phonetic realisation of the accent and argues for a starless LH accent
evidence_works.loc: pp. 307 (section 2, stress and intonation in Persian), 311-312 (materials and measurements), 322-323 (discussion), 325 (conclusion)
evidence_works.venue: Journal of the International Phonetic Association

evidence_works.work: Jones, William (1809). A Grammar of the Persian Language. Low Price Publications.
evidence_works.detail: One sentence only: word accent 'usually' on the last syllable (final stress), with no rule for exceptions, no statement of secondary stress (the 'strong accent upon every fourth syllable' is verse scansion of a Meninski couplet, not lexical secondary stress), and no mention of tone or pitch. Syllable weight (vowels long by nature; short syllable closed by a consonant long by position) is described only as metrical quantity for prosody, not as a stress conditioner. The grammar describes the literary (classical) Persian of the 18t
